quiz.question: What is the primary difference between authentication and authorization?
options: Authentication assigns roles; authorization validates passwords
Authentication verifies identity; authorization determines permitted actions
Authentication and authorization are interchangeable terms
Authorization is only required for administrators
quiz.explanation: Authentication verifies the identity claim of a user or principal (Who are you?). Authorization decides whether that authenticated identity is permitted to perform a requested operation on a specific resource (What are you allowed to do?).

quiz.question: Which combination qualifies as MFA?
options: Password and security question
Two different passwords
A password and an authenticator using a distinct factor category
Username and email address
quiz.explanation: True Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) requires factors from at least two distinct categories: something you know (password/PIN), something you have (cryptographic security key/passkey), or something you are (biometric). Two passwords or a password + security question are both knowledge factors and do not constitute MFA.

quiz.question: What is privilege creep?
options: Permissions accumulate as responsibilities change without appropriate removal
All user permissions are removed after every login
A system encrypts stored credentials
A user chooses a new password
quiz.explanation: Privilege creep occurs when users change teams, projects, or roles over time (the 'mover' lifecycle stage) and receive new permissions while their previous entitlements are never revoked, resulting in excessive, unneeded access.

quiz.question: Which statement about OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect is correct?
options: OAuth 2.0 is a complete user-authentication protocol in every implementation
OAuth 2.0 primarily handles delegated authorization; OpenID Connect adds an identity layer
OpenID Connect is a Linux access-control mechanism
They are encryption algorithms
quiz.explanation: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework designed for delegated API access (using Access Tokens). OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an identity layer built on top of OAuth 2.0 that standardizes user authentication and provides identity claims via ID Tokens.

quiz.question: Which is a strong authorization design for private user reports?
options: Hide the reports button from other users only in the frontend
Allow any signed-in user to request any report identifier
Check resource ownership or approved permissions on the trusted server side
Trust the user ID supplied by the browser without verification
quiz.explanation: To prevent Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR / BOLA), the server must independently verify the authenticated user's session and enforce relationship- or role-based ownership checks on every request, rather than trusting client-side parameters.

quiz.question: Which authentication approach is designed to provide phishing resistance?
options: Properly implemented FIDO passkeys or security-key authentication
Reusing the same password across services
Approving all unexpected MFA push requests
Sending passwords through email
quiz.explanation: FIDO2 / WebAuthn passkeys and hardware security keys use public-key cryptography bound directly to the browser's verified TLS origin. An attacker's fake phishing proxy cannot replay or intercept the authentication assertion.

theorySections.title: Identity and Access Management Fundamentals
paragraphs: Digital identities, proofing, authentication vs authorization, accounting/auditing, principals, and the principle of least privilege under NIST SP 800-63-4.

Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the combination of policies, processes, technologies, and controls used to establish digital identities, verify claims about those identities, grant appropriate access, and remove access when it is no longer justified.

theorySections.title: Identity Lifecycle and Identity Governance
paragraphs: The Joiner-Mover-Leaver (JML) paradigm, preventing privilege creep, automated deprovisioning, and recurring access certifications.
Identity proofing, HR approval, birthright role assignment, and initial MFA authenticator enrollment.
Role transition review. Explicitly revoke previous entitlements before assigning new ones to prevent privilege creep.
Immediate account suspension, refresh token revocation, device certificate wipe, and resource ownership transfer.

Privilege creep occurs when an employee accumulates permissions across multiple department changes over years without old rights being pruned. An employee who worked in Helpdesk, then Development, then DevOps might inadvertently retain direct Active Directory password reset rights, production code deployment rights, and cloud administrative credentials simultaneously.

theorySections.title: Authentication Fundamentals and Password Security
paragraphs: Authentication factors (Know, Have, Are), password attack vectors, NIST SP 800-63B-4 modern password standards, and adaptive hashing (Argon2id, bcrypt).
Password, passphrase, PIN. Subject to credential stuffing and phishing.
Hardware security key (YubiKey), smartphone authenticator, cryptographic smartcard.
Biometric template: fingerprint sensor, facial recognition matching local secure enclave.

theorySections.title: Multifactor Authentication and Phishing-Resistant Access
paragraphs: MFA mechanisms, why two passwords is NOT MFA, MFA fatigue attacks, and CISA recommendations on FIDO2/WebAuthn origin-bound passkeys.

theorySections.title: Authorization Models and Access Control
paragraphs: Discretionary (DAC), Mandatory (MAC), Role-Based (RBAC), Attribute-Based (ABAC), and Relationship-Based (ReBAC) access control models.
Assigns permissions to roles (e.g. Student, Instructor, Admin), and subjects to those roles. Standard for coarse-grained enterprise workflows.
Evaluates attributes of user (department, clearance), resource (classification), action (read, delete), and environment (time, device IP).
Evaluates dynamic relationships (e.g. user IS_OWNER_OF report_101 or instructor IN_CHARGE_OF course_3). Prevents IDOR.

theorySections.title: Single Sign-On, Federation, OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, and SAML
paragraphs: Architectural comparison of SSO, OAuth 2.0 delegated authorization, OpenID Connect authentication tokens, and SAML XML assertions.

theorySections.title: Session Security, Privileged Access, and Non-Human Identities
paragraphs: Cookie security flags (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite), Privileged Access Management (PAM), Just-In-Time (JIT) access, and service account workload identities.
